name: Oxybenzone
lead: Oxybenzone (benzophenone-3, BP-3) is an organic UV filter that absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA, used in sunscreens, lip products, hair sprays, nail polish and as a stabiliser in plastics [1][2]. It was first synthesised in 1906 by Bernhard König and Stanisław Kostanecki and later developed as a sunscreen ingredient from the 1950s, according to Grokipedia [1][2].

It is one of the most debated sunscreen ingredients. Biomonitoring found it in about 97% of US urine samples tested in 2003-2004 [3], clinical trials show it is absorbed through the skin [4], and laboratory work links it to coral damage [5]. Several jurisdictions, including Hawaii, have banned sales of sunscreens containing it [2]. In the United States the FDA classes it as not yet shown to be generally recognised as safe and effective because of insufficient data, while it remains legal [2].

paras: Oxybenzone is an organic, chemical UV filter: it absorbs ultraviolet light and dissipates it, and is grouped with the organic filters, in contrast to the inorganic filters zinc oxide and titanium dioxide.[1][2][20] Reviews describe broad-spectrum protection, covering both UVB and UVA, as the aim of sunscreen use for preventing sunburn, photoaging and skin cancer.[21] Photoprotection is also part of how people manage uneven pigmentation, and a registered trial examined UV and visible-light protection in the treatment of melasma.[24]

Sunscreen filters can be added to foundations and tinted products, which is how oxybenzone reaches people who think of the product as makeup rather than sun protection.[6] Wikipedia reports that the share of US sunscreens containing it fell from 60 percent in 2019 to 13 percent in 2023 as brands reformulated.[2]

Oxybenzone is valued by formulators for broad UV absorption, absorbing between 270 and 350 nm with peaks near 288 and 350 nm [2]. Grokipedia reports it was found in roughly 70% of sunscreens by the 1990s, while Wikipedia reports the share of US sunscreens containing it fell from 60% in 2019 to 13% in 2023 [1][2]. It also appears in foundations, such as a labelled US cosmetic product combining it with octinoxate [6].

Wikipedia summarises studies estimating that 0.4% to 8.7% of a topical dose is absorbed after one application, with higher absorption possible with repeated use [2]. A US survey (NHANES 2003-2004) reported benzophenone-3 concentrations in residents, detected in about 97% of urine samples [3][2]. Pregnancy cohorts measured urinary phenols including benzophenone-3 in relation to birth outcomes and offspring size [7][8], and a Puerto Rico study examined urinary phenol levels in pregnant women [9]. A 2020 JAMA randomised trial found oxybenzone in plasma after sunscreen use [4].

A 2025 review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology traces the US Food and Drug Administration's regulation of sunscreen and notes that FDA studies show organic filters are systemically absorbed during routine use, while stating that to date no associated negative health effects have been shown.[18] The FDA's guidance referenced in a 2019 JAMA trial sets a plasma level of 0.5 ng/mL above which nonclinical toxicology assessment is recommended.[22] The 2020 JAMA trial measured plasma levels of six active ingredients in four products under single and maximal use.[4] In the United States, Wikipedia reports that oxybenzone has not been classified as generally recognised as safe and effective because of insufficient data, while it remains on the market.[2]

Reviews describe endocrine-related activity in laboratory assays [10][11]. A mini-review summarised occurrence, toxicity and ecological risk [12]. Wikipedia reports that photoallergic reactions are uncommon, though it is described as a frequent sunscreen allergen, and that Sweden's research council concluded it is unsuitable for children under two [2]. In September 2025 the European Chemicals Agency identified it as an endocrine disruptor, according to Wikipedia [2].

A review of zinc oxide and titanium dioxide describes them as inorganic filters with broad UV absorption (zinc oxide) or better UVB protection (titanium dioxide), with very little skin absorption.[20] The same review says nanoparticle forms are less visible on the skin and recommends against nanoparticle spray products because of inhalation concerns.[20] Products labelled mineral use these inorganic filters instead of organic ones such as oxybenzone.

A 2016 study reported toxic effects on coral larvae and cultured coral cells and measured contamination in Hawaii and the US Virgin Islands [5]. Wikipedia notes that critics say many studies lacked controls or realistic conditions [2]. Sales bans or restrictions exist in Hawaii (2021), the US Virgin Islands (2020), Aruba and Bonaire (2019), Palau (2020), and marine parks in Thailand, while Florida's 2020 law preempted a local ban in Key West [2].

Clinical work centres on absorption and tolerability. A 2019 randomised trial under maximal-use conditions examined whether avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene and ecamsule from four commercial sunscreens were absorbed into the bloodstream, measured against the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold.[22] A 2020 JAMA trial in 48 healthy participants, randomised to a lotion or one of three spray formats, measured six filters including oxybenzone to assess absorption and how quickly systemic exposure exceeds 0.5 ng/mL.[4] The phase 1 absorption study NCT03582215 enrolled 72 participants.[13]

A 2023 comprehensive review and meta-analysis of human biomonitoring studies, carried out for the Human Biomonitoring for Europe initiative, screened 1,635 titles and tabulated 254 references on exposure, toxicokinetics and health outcomes.[17] Photoallergy has been examined in a 1,000-participant European photopatch study.[14][23] Several small SPF-testing studies of sunscreen products list oxybenzone-era formulations.[15] Biomonitoring and exposure-reduction trials, including a 1,074-participant report-back intervention, address endocrine-disrupting chemical exposure generally.[16] No trial tests oxybenzone alone for appearance outcomes.

Oxybenzone appears in skincare conversation mainly through the chemical versus mineral sunscreen debate. Proponents of avoiding it point to biomonitoring, endocrine-activity and coral findings, while dermatology reviews describe sunscreen as important for preventing skin cancer and photoaging and report no demonstrated harm from absorption to date.[18][19][21]

timeline.event: First synthesised by König and Kostanecki [2].

card.summary: A broad-spectrum sunscreen filter found in most people's urine, linked to reef-damage findings and banned in places like Hawaii, yet still legal under US federal rules.
card.note: Banned in Hawaii and several other jurisdictions; EU limits apply.

quick.overview:
Oxybenzone is an organic sunscreen filter that absorbs both UVB and part of UVA light. It was long among the most common sunscreen ingredients, though its use in US sunscreens has declined.

It is controversial because it is absorbed into the body, detected in most people tested in a US survey, and linked in lab studies to coral damage.
quick.mechanism: Its aromatic ketone structure absorbs UV photons between about 270 and 350 nm and releases the energy as heat [1][2].
quick.risks: Reported issues include skin allergy, systemic absorption, endocrine activity in lab assays and coral toxicity findings. Hawaii, the US Virgin Islands, Palau, Aruba and others restrict it; the FDA lists it as lacking sufficient safety data but it remains legal.

chain: Absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA in the formula
Slower photoaging, sunburn and uneven pigmentation over time
angle.text: Oxybenzone is one of the UV filters that lets a sunscreen, tinted moisturiser or foundation protect skin from sun exposure. Daily photoprotection is how people look to keep skin tone even and limit sun-related aging, and the filter is one way a product delivers it.
